entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 13
 
Ge 13:1-18. Return from Egypt.

1. went up ... south--Palestine being a highland country, the entrance from Egypt by its southern boundary is a continual ascent.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv152"/><div sID="gen308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv152"/><hi type="bold">2. very rich--</hi>compared with the pastoral tribes to which Abraham belonged. An Arab sheik is considered rich who has a hundred or two hundred tents, from sixty to a hundred camels, a thousand sheep and goats respectively. And Abram being very rich, must have far exceeded that amount of pastoral property. "Gold and silver" being rare among these peoples, his probably arose from the sale of his produce in Egypt. <div eID="gen308" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv154"/><div sID="gen311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv154"/><hi type="bold">4. there Abram called on the name of the Lord--</hi>He felt a strong desire to reanimate his faith and piety on the scene of his former worship: it might be to express humility and penitence for his misconduct in Egypt or thankfulness for deliverance from perils--to embrace the first opportunity on returning to Canaan of leading his family to renew allegiance to God and offer the typical sacrifices which pointed to the blessings of the promise. <div eID="gen311" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv155"/><div sID="gen312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv155"/><hi type="bold">7. And there was a strife--</hi>Abraham's character appears here in a most amiable light. Having a strong sense of religion, he was afraid of doing anything that might tend to injure its character or bring discredit on its name, and he rightly judged that such unhappy effects would be produced if two persons whom nature and grace had so closely connected should come to a rupture [Ge 13:8]. Waiving his right to dictate, he gave the freedom of choice to Lot. The conduct of Abraham was not only disinterested and peaceable, but generous and condescending in an extraordinary degree, exemplifying the Scripture precepts (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.32">Mt 6:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.10">Ro 12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.4">Php 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen312" type="x-p"/>
